title: Solve Multiple Percent Equations with List Regression
description: Translate connected percent and percent-change statements with Desmos % of notation, pair them in one list regression, and repair a zero-out fit only when it occurs.

blocks.html:
Give it a try

Spend about a minute on this question. Keep what you tried, even if you got stuck. You can continue without submitting an answer.

shared_prompt.title: Three related samples
shared_prompt.html:
Samples R, S, and T have positive masses. The mass of R is \(75\%\) of the combined mass of S and T. The mass of S is \(20\%\) of the combined mass of R and T.

The mass of T is \(p\%\) of the combined mass of R and S. What is the value of \(p\)?

content.html:
Let the percent statements work together

In the opening question, each percentage uses a combined mass, and the unknown amounts depend on one another. Solving the statements one at a time would require several rearrangements.

One list regression can connect them as written. We’ll refresh the paired-list entry, then add the percent statements.

Refresh the matching pairs

For \(a+b=11\) and \(a-b=3\), \([a+b,a-b]\sim[11,3]\) matches first to first and second to second. The tilde, ~, asks Desmos to find the unknowns. This is list regression.

content.hint: Keep each equation’s sides in matching positions, then check the symbol between the lists.
content.prompt: Which single row pairs \(A+B=18\) and \(A-B=6\) correctly?
content.explanation: The first pair says \(A+B=18\); the second says \(A-B=6\). The tilde fits their unknowns together.

content.html:
Translate “percent of” directly

“A is 240% of B” becomes \(A=240\%\text{ of }B\). The amount after “of” is the base of the comparison.

In Desmos, typing % inserts “of” automatically. Type the base after it. Keep decimal percents such as 0.8% as written.

content.hint: Identify the mass being described, then the mass named after “of.”
content.prompt: A sample’s mass A is 0.8% of mass C. Which equation translates that statement?
content.explanation: A is the described mass; C is the base. Keep 0.8% as written. The other entries reverse the comparison, add an increase, or change the percent.

content.html:
Make the question an equation too

The requested percent is another unknown. For “C is p% of B,” write \(C=p\%\text{ of }B\).

Include that equation alongside the given comparisons so regression can find the requested percent directly.

Put the statements in one regression

Define \(B=50\). Enter \([A,A,C]\sim[240\%\text{ of }B,0.8\%\text{ of }C,p\%\text{ of }B]\). Desmos finds \(p=30000\).

RMSE measures the mismatch between paired sides. For exact equations, look for zero or a tiny value and amounts that fit the problem.

shared_prompt.title: Connected percent statements
shared_prompt.html: Sample A is 240% of sample B and 0.8% of sample C. Sample B has mass 50 grams. If C is p% of B, find p.

content.hint: Translate the question using the same “is” and “of” order as a given statement.
content.prompt: The question asks: “C is p% of B.” Which equation belongs in the paired lists?
content.explanation: C is the described amount, p is the unknown percent, and B is its base. Reversing B and C changes the comparison.

content.html:
Translate, then Pair

  1. Translate each comparison, including the question.
  2. Keep any given measurement.
  3. Pair matching sides with one tilde.
  4. Inspect the amounts and RMSE, then read the requested value.

content.title: Translate, then pair

feedback.solution_html: Keep \(B=40\). Enter \([A,A,C]\sim[150\%\text{ of }B,25\%\text{ of }C,p\%\text{ of }B]\). Desmos fits \(A=60,C=240,p=600\).
feedback.retry_message_html: Keep B=40. Check the order of the three percent entries, including which amount follows each “of.”
feedback.success_message_html: Nice work! The three percent statements are paired correctly. Read p and check the fit.

content.instructions_html: Keep \(B=40\). Enter one list regression for A being 150% of B, A being 25% of C, and C being p% of B. Use \([A,A,C]\) on the left and matching percent expressions on the right.

shared_prompt.title: Find the requested percent
shared_prompt.html: Sample A is 150% of sample B and 25% of sample C. Sample B has mass 40 grams. If C is p% of B, find p.

content.hint: Read the fitted parameter for the requested percent, rather than one of the fitted amounts.
content.prompt: In the problem you just entered, A is 150% of B, A is 25% of C, and B is 40. If C is p% of B, what is p?
content.solution:
Enter \(B=40\), then \([A,A,C]\sim[150\%\text{ of }B,25\%\text{ of }C,p\%\text{ of }B]\).
Read \(p=600\) under REGRESSION PARAMETERS. Report 600, not C or C/B.
content.explanation: The fitted p is 600. C is six times B, which is 600% of B.

content.html:
What if no mass is given?

The ratios can fix the requested percent even when the individual masses can vary. Try the three-pair regression without defining a mass first. If it gives positive masses that satisfy the statements and zero or tiny RMSE, read \(p\).

If the masses all become zero

Zero masses make every entered comparison read zero equals zero, regardless of \(p\). That fit cannot determine the percent.

If this happens and no mass was supplied, define one free base, such as \(B=1\), and refit. Scaling all masses together preserves their percent comparisons.

content.hint: The result already satisfies the equations and the positive-mass context.
content.prompt: With no given mass, Desmos returns positive masses that satisfy every percent statement and zero RMSE. What should you do?
choices: Replace every fitted mass with 1 and run again.
Define B=1 before using any fitted percent.
Report RMSE as the requested percent value.
Read the requested percent from the fitted p.
content.explanation: A valid positive fit already answers the question. Setting a free base is a response to a zero-out result, not a required first step.

content.hint: A free reference amount sets the scale. The other amounts and the requested percent still need to satisfy the relationships.
content.prompt: No actual mass is given. Your percent equations return A=B=C=0, although the samples have positive masses. What is the appropriate repair?
choices: Accept p because the RMSE is zero.
Set one free mass, such as B, to 1 and refit.
Set every mass to 1 and keep the same p.
Replace the requested percent p with 1 and refit.
content.explanation: Fix one free positive base and let the other values refit. Defining every mass would conflict with the comparisons; fixing p would choose the answer.

content.html:
Keep a supplied mass

If the question gives a mass, use that measurement in its definition. It is no longer a free base.

Choosing a reference amount helps with relative comparisons; it cannot replace a stated measurement.

content.hint: Use the measurement supplied by the question.
content.prompt: A percent-equations problem gives B=75 grams. Which definition should the calculator use?
content.explanation: Keep B=75. A convenient reference value cannot replace an actual stated quantity.

content.html:
Keep the base in “greater than” and “less than”

“A is 20% greater than B” becomes \(A=B+20\%\text{ of }B\). “A is 25% less than C” becomes \(A=C-25\%\text{ of }C\).

The amount after “than” is the base. Include that original amount as well as its change.

content.hint: Start with the amount named after “than,” then subtract a percent of that same amount.
content.prompt: A is 25% less than C. Which equation preserves the base and the remaining amount?
content.explanation: Start with C and subtract 25% of C. The other choices keep just the removed part, use A as the base, or make an increase.

content.html:
Only the expressions change

Pair those statements the same way:

\[[A,A,C]\sim[B+20\%\text{ of }B,C-25\%\text{ of }C,p\%\text{ of }B]\]

Inspect the positive amounts and RMSE. If the free masses all become zero, define \(B=1\) and refit.

shared_prompt.title: Connected percent changes
shared_prompt.html: A is 20% greater than B and 25% less than C. All three amounts are positive. If C is p% of B, find p.

blocks.html:
A combined amount is one base

“A is \(30\%\) of the combined mass of B and C” becomes \(A=30\%\text{ of }(B+C)\).

Put the whole sum in parentheses after “of.” The rest of Translate, then Pair stays the same.

content.prompt: A is \(30\%\) of the combined mass of B and C. Which entry keeps the complete base?
content.hint: The percent applies to the combined mass. Keep everything in that combined amount grouped after “of.”
content.solution:
The base is the sum \(B+C\).
Put parentheses around that sum: \(A=30\%\text{ of }(B+C)\).
content.explanation: C keeps the combined mass together. Without those parentheses, the entry adds all of C after taking a percent of B.

blocks.html:
Return to the three samples

Try the opening question again. Translate the linked comparisons and find the requested percent.

content.hint: Treat each combined mass as one parenthesized base. Include the requested percent as another paired equation, then inspect the amounts and RMSE. Repair a zero-mass fit if needed.
content.solution:
Enter \([R,S,T]\sim[75\%\text{ of }(S+T),20\%\text{ of }(R+T),p\%\text{ of }(R+S)]\).
Read p only from positive masses with zero or tiny RMSE.
If the masses all become zero, define a free mass, such as \(T=100\), and refit.
At that scale, \(R\approx105.882353,\ S\approx41.176471\), and \(p=68\).
Report \(68\).
content.explanation: You found \(p=68\). One regression connected all three comparisons while keeping each combined mass as its own percent base.

content.prompt: Recall “translate, then pair.” Which routine carries several percent statements through to an answer?
choices: Translate with % of; pair matching sides with ~; check the amounts; report RMSE as the requested percent.
Translate with % of; pair sides in separate orders with ~; check the fit and read the requested value.
Translate with % of; pair matching sides with ~; check the fit and read the requested value; repair a zero-out result if needed.
Translate with % of; fix each unknown amount at 1; pair matching sides with ~; check the fit and read the requested value.
content.explanation: Translate each comparison, including the requested one. Matching list positions preserve the statements. Inspect the fit before making any manual assignment, and preserve given quantities.

blocks.html:
Try it on your own

Choose the approach for each question. Try these now or save them for homework.

content.prompt: A is 50% greater than B and 20% less than C. All three quantities are positive. If C is p% of B, what is the value of p?
content.explanation: Enter \([A,A,C]\sim[B+50\%\text{ of }B,C-20\%\text{ of }C,p\%\text{ of }B]\). Inspect the fit; if the amounts zero out, define the free base \(B=1\) and rerun. A valid positive fit gives \(p=187.5\).

content.html:
Translate, then Pair

Use the comparison’s base and keep the related statements in one regression.
